name: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together: NHS view
headline: Can you take ibuprofen and paracetamol together? What the NHS says
summary: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, but suggests trying each alone first and checking first in some cases.
keyPoints: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, though trying each on its own first is a good idea.
For children, the NHS says not to give ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time unless a doctor advises it.
The NHS lists groups who should check with a doctor or pharmacist before ibuprofen, including people with stomach ulcers, asthma or kidney problems.
Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol, ibuprofen or both, so using several products can lead to taking too much without meaning to.
For urgent worries call NHS 111, and call 999 for emergencies such as signs of a serious allergic reaction.

body.heading: What is each medicine used for?
body.body: Ibuprofen belongs to a group of painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS says it can help with headaches and migraines, joint and muscle pain, pain after an injury, toothache and period pain. It also treats inflammation and can bring down a fever. Paracetamol is a painkiller used for pain and a high temperature. The NHS notes that ibuprofen can cause more side effects than paracetamol, so trying paracetamol first is a good idea for people who can take it.

body.heading: Can adults take both at the same time?
body.body: For adults, the NHS says paracetamol can be taken at the same time as ibuprofen if needed. It also suggests trying each medicine on its own first, to see whether one is enough to ease the pain. NHS inform, the NHS information service for Scotland, also says the two can be taken together if required. For dental pain, it says taking both can help when one alone is not enough. The advice is different for children. For them, the NHS says not to give ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time, and to give one at a time unless a doctor advises otherwise. This guide is about adults.

body.heading: Who is told to check with a pharmacist or doctor first?
body.body:
The NHS lists several groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check with a professional before using it. These include people who have had an allergic reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs, with signs such as wheezing, a runny nose or skin reactions. They also include people who have had stomach bleeding or ulcers caused by an NSAID, and people with severe heart, kidney or liver failure. Asthma, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are also on the NHS list of conditions to mention first. The NHS also says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor when breastfeeding. People over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen, according to the NHS.

Some other medicines also matter. The NHS says to tell a doctor before starting ibuprofen when taking blood thinners such as warfarin, blood pressure medicines, steroids, some antibiotics, antidepressants or diabetes medicines. For paracetamol, the NHS names warfarin, epilepsy medicines and tuberculosis medicines as ones to discuss with a doctor, along with metoclopramide, domperidone and the antibiotic flucloxacillin. NHS inform advises people who take other medication or have other health conditions to check with a pharmacist first.

body.heading: Why do other products containing the same ingredients matter?
body.body: Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol, ibuprofen or both. NHS inform says this makes it easy to go over the limit by accident. The NHS says to avoid taking other medicines that contain paracetamol at the same time as paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies, because too much can be dangerous. It adds that too much paracetamol can cause liver damage. For ibuprofen, the NHS says to check the label of cold and cough remedies for aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Taking ibuprofen with other NSAIDs such as aspirin or naproxen is not advised without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor, because side effects such as stomach ache become more likely.

body.heading: What side effects do the NHS pages describe?
body.body:
The NHS lists common side effects of ibuprofen as indigestion, stomach aches, nausea and headaches. Serious ones include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, and allergic reactions. The NHS says the risk is higher with high doses or long-term use. Taking ibuprofen with or after food makes stomach upset less likely, the NHS says. NHS inform adds that ibuprofen may make asthma worse. For paracetamol, the NHS says there may be no obvious symptoms at first after taking too much, so feeling well does not rule out harm.

The NHS page lists side effects but says its list is not complete, and points to the leaflet in the medicine pack. Side effects can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.

body.heading: When should someone get help, and from whom?
body.body:
For signs of a serious allergic reaction to ibuprofen, such as swollen lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing or a tight throat, the NHS says to call 999. Black poo or blood in vomit can mean bleeding in the stomach, and the NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. Severe chest or stomach pain needs 999 or A&E, the NHS says, because it can signal a hole in the stomach or gut. Swollen ankles, blood in urine or passing no urine can point to a kidney problem, and the NHS says to call 111 or a doctor.

If too much paracetamol has been taken, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice, even when the person feels well. Severe tummy pain, vomiting, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, confusion or passing no urine are listed as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E. For questions that are not urgent, such as whether a mix of medicines suits someone with other conditions, NHS inform points to a pharmacist, and a GP can also advise.
